S1.title: Python Debugging Playbook
S1.text:
4. Performance Pitfalls
functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128) caches the results of a function for repeated arguments; the
default maxsize is 128 and maxsize=None removes the limit. Arguments must be hashable.
Building a long string with += inside a loop copies the string repeatedly; collect the pieces in a list
and call "".join(parts) once. A membership test with in is a linear scan for a list but an average
constant-time lookup for a set or dict, so convert a list to a set when you test membership many
times.
collections.Counter(words).most_common(3) returns the three most frequent items as (item, count)
pairs. Sorting with sorted(items, key=len) is faster and clearer than writing a comparison function.

S4.title: Python Debugging Playbook
S4.text:
2. Scope Errors
UnboundLocalError (message: local variable referenced before assignment) happens when a
function assigns to a name anywhere in its body, which makes that name local for the entire
function, and then reads the name before the assignment has run. The usual symptom is code that
works at module level but fails once it is moved inside a function.
Three fixes exist. Pass the value in as a parameter, which is the cleanest option. Use the global
statement to bind a module-level name. Use the nonlocal statement to bind a name from the
nearest enclosing function scope; nonlocal cannot reach module-level names.
A related surprise is the late-binding closure: lambdas created in a loop all see the final value of the
loop variable. The fix is to bind the current value through a default argument, for example lambda
i=i: i.

S5.title: Python Lecture Notes
S5.text: 3. Functions A function is a reusable block of code defined with def. Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the values supplied in a call. A function returns a value with return; if no return statement runs, the function returns None. Default parameter values, as in def greet(name, greeting="Hello"), let callers omit an argument. Keyword arguments, as in greet(greeting="Hi", name="Sara"), make calls explicit. *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. Never use a mutable object such as a list as a default value. The default is created once when the function is defined, so def add(x, bucket=[]) shares one list across all calls. The safe pattern is bucket=None followed by if bucket is None: bucket = []. Variables created inside a function are local to it.
